sections.h2: Does Missouri tax the profit when you sell a house?
sections.html:
For individuals, Missouri now lets you subtract 100 percent of federally reported capital gains from federal adjusted gross income on the state return, so the profit on a house sale is effectively not taxed by Missouri. The authority is Section 143.121 RSMo, added by House Bill 594.

The Missouri Department of Revenue announced the change on August 26, 2025, describing Missouri as the first state to fully exempt capital gains tax for individual filers. The release says individuals can deduct all capital gains reported for federal purposes, short term and long term, from assets such as stocks, real estate and cryptocurrency, effective January 1, 2025. Federal tax is a separate matter and still applies to the gain.

sections.h2: How do you claim the Missouri capital gains subtraction?
sections.html:
You claim it on Form MO-A, filed with your Form MO-1040 individual income tax return. The amount comes from the capital gain portion of your federal return. For the 2025 tax year the department says the figure is the amount on line 7a of federal Form 1040.

One wrinkle needs attention. The department's FAQ opens by calling the subtraction effective for the 2025 tax year, yet a later answer says it applies to tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026 and can first be claimed on the 2026 return filed in 2027. If you sold a house in 2025, confirm with the department which return carries the subtraction before you file.

Married couples need care when only one spouse has a gain. The department's example shows a combined $10,000 on line 7a made of a $5,000 loss for one spouse and a $15,000 gain for the other. The $10,000 goes on the MO-A line for the spouse who had the gain, and nothing goes on the other spouse's line.

sections.h2: Who cannot use the Missouri subtraction?
sections.html:
The subtraction is written for individuals subject to tax under section 143.011. The department's answers draw several lines:

  • Trusts cannot claim it, because a fiduciary is not an individual subject to that section.
  • A pass-through entity that pays pass-through entity tax cannot claim it.
  • Corporations are excluded for now. They may subtract 100 percent of capital gains in the tax year after Missouri's top individual rate falls to 4.5 percent or lower, and the top rate for 2025 is 4.7 percent.
  • Capital losses do not qualify. The subtraction reaches only federally reported capital gains, and allowed losses already reduce federal adjusted gross income.

If your house is held in a trust or an LLC taxed as a pass-through, talk to a tax preparer before you list it.

sections.h2: What federal tax is due on a Missouri house sale?
sections.html:
The IRS lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain on the sale of your main home, or up to $500,000 on a joint return. You qualify by meeting both an ownership test and a use test: you owned the home at least 24 months and used it as a residence for at least 24 months during the 5 years before the sale. The two periods can fall in different stretches. Generally you cannot use the exclusion if you excluded gain from another home sale within the prior two years.

If you get a Form 1099-S you must report the sale even when the gain is fully excludable. When some gain is taxable, report it on Form 8949 and Schedule D. The IRS says the tax rate on most net long-term gain is no higher than 15 percent for most individuals in 2025, with 0 percent at lower incomes and 20 percent at the top. Gain held one year or less is short term and taxed as ordinary income. Depreciation recapture on a rental, called unrecaptured section 1250 gain, tops out at 25 percent.

Because Missouri follows your federal figures, an accurate federal return is the starting point for everything on the state side.

sections.h2: Do estimated payments or surtaxes follow a large home sale?
sections.html:
A taxable gain on a house can trigger a quarterly estimated tax obligation on the federal side, since the IRS says a taxpayer with a taxable capital gain may be required to make estimated payments. Its Publication 505 explains how to decide whether you must. Individuals with significant investment income can also owe the net investment income tax, which the IRS describes in Topic 559.

Losses work differently. The IRS does not allow a deduction for a loss on a home you lived in. For other capital assets, a net capital loss can reduce income by up to $3,000 a year ($1,500 if married filing separately), with the rest carried forward. A seller who lived in the house and is selling at a loss has nothing to claim for the house itself, and the Missouri subtraction cannot turn a loss into a deduction either.

Sellers who rented out the house for part of their ownership should ask a preparer how the rental years affect the exclusion and any depreciation recapture before listing.

sections.h2: How is the gain figured when you inherited the house?
sections.html:
Gain is the sale price less your adjusted basis. For an inherited house, IRS Publication 551 says basis is generally the fair market value on the date of death, or on the alternate valuation date if the estate chose one. When the estate had to file a federal estate tax return, the executor gives beneficiaries a Schedule A on Form 8971 showing the value to use. Keep the appraisal or the date-of-death value with your records.

The IRS notes that basis can also change with improvements you add and with depreciation you claimed. For holding period questions on property acquired from a decedent, IRS Topic 409 points to Publication 544.

sections.h2: What steps should a Missouri seller take before filing?
sections.html:
• Collect the closing disclosure and any Form 1099-S from the title company.
  • Add up your purchase price, closing costs at purchase and capital improvements to build the adjusted basis.
  • Test the federal exclusion with the 24 month ownership and use rules.
  • Report the sale on the federal return if the gain exceeds the exclusion or if you received a 1099-S.
  • Carry the federal capital gain amount to Form MO-A and claim the subtraction on MO-1040.
  • Check withholding. The Department of Revenue's release suggests preparers review client withholding and consider lowering it where the new subtraction applies.

Keep these records for as long as you may need to defend the return.

faqs.q: Does Missouri have a capital gains tax on real estate?
faqs.a: Not for individuals who qualify for the subtraction. Missouri lets eligible individuals subtract 100 percent of federally reported capital gains, including real estate gains, from federal adjusted gross income. You still report the sale on your federal return.

faqs.q: Which Missouri form do I use to claim the capital gains subtraction?
faqs.a: Form MO-A, filed with Form MO-1040. The capital gain amount comes from your federal return, which for 2025 is line 7a of Form 1040.

faqs.q: Can a trust or LLC claim the Missouri subtraction?
faqs.a: Generally no. The Department of Revenue says a trust is not an individual subject to tax under section 143.011, and a pass-through entity subject to pass-through entity tax cannot claim it either.

faqs.q: How much of my home sale gain can I exclude on my federal return?
faqs.a: Up to $250,000, or up to $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the home for at least 24 months of the last 5 years. The IRS covers the details in Topic 701 and Publication 523.

faqs.q: Does the Missouri subtraction cover a capital loss on my house?
faqs.a: No. The department states capital losses do not qualify for the subtraction, and the IRS says a loss on the sale of a personal residence is not deductible.
